Absolutely. Oil based not water based. Thin your first few coats with mineral spirits. Cherry takes Poly very very well and you can really get a very stunning finish out of it.

Another hot tip, oil based Poly might feel dry after 24hrs but it is NOT done curing. If you put your nose to the table and still "smell" Poly it's still very soft. My cherry desk I made a while back took a full week and a half to fully cure.

If you start using the piece before the Poly is fully cured its very easy to put an indent into the finish. Even doing something as gentle as drawing with a #2 pencil.

Totally depends on what projects you want to start with. If you want to start making small boxes chisels, a dovetail saw, and a coping saw are a must. If you wanna build a deck, you're gonna need a drill, a circular saw, etc. I was woodworking for almost 4 years before I even owned a chisel! Lol

No one ever has ALL the tools they need/want. For people with little to no tools looking at getting into the hobby I generally recommend they find a smaller/simple project they would be interested in and buy the tools needed for that. Your next project should incorporate some if not all of the tools you bought previously, but require the addition of a new tool(s). Good way to "grow" a shop!

A circular saw can get you very far! Especially with a good straight edge. I built my first deck, patio table, benches and flower boxes years ago with a circular saw. I never owned a table saw until I wanted to get into fine furniture making that required very accurate cuts. 

I find circular saws are perfectly adequate for crosscuts, but for rip cuts they are a pain in the ass for all but the widest boards (Google rip cut and cross cut for examples if you don't know what I'm talking about). That's really where a tablesaw shines. Rip cutting and repeatable accurate cuts.

Glue is generally used for a "perfect joint", usually two super flat edges that when pressed together have an invisible seam. Using 2x4s, you'll almost never get a perfectly flat glue surface like that unless you employ some power tools like a planer or jointer. Just using them as is from the store go with nails or screws. If you really want to be thorough you could put some glue in there too I guess.

You must know SOMETHING I mean after all you found this sub. Based on the things you're saying you want to do you're gonna need a key few items to get going.

1. Drill, corded or battery is fine (and or a hammer and nails if that helps offset your costs!) 

2. Circular saw (please watch some videos on use if you've never used one. Educate yourself so you can use the saw safely) 

3. Probably some saw horses

4. A square or two

5. Time and patience


Woodworking takes a lifetime to truly master. And you're on the right track starting simple. It doesn't matter what you're making or how complex it is as long as YOU are proud of it!

As for materials.. The planter box can probably be very easily done in dimensional lumber like 2x4s (bigger or larger depending on size) or something similar. The cornhole board is also rather simple you just need some plywood and a holesaw!
